tip: Times of day usually take को (ko), not में: शाम को (shaam ko = to evening) means in the evening. Subah ko, raat ko – no equivalent of the English in appears.
Next to is a body word: सुरेश के बगल में (Suresh ke bagal mein = in Suresh's side) – bagal is your side or flank. Many Hindi place phrases sit inside a noun like this.
Hindi builds before as from + earlier: दशहरे से पहले (Dashahre se pahle = from Dussehra earlier) = before Dussehra. After uses के not से: दशहरे के बाद (ke baad).
पर (par) usually means on or at, but after a verb form it means upon: छींक आने पर (chheenk aane par = on a sneeze coming) = when you sneeze.
Seeing the doctor is showing: डॉक्टर को दिखाना है (doctor ko dikhaana hai = have to show to the doctor). You show yourself to doctors in Hindi – dikhaana, not dekhna.
Hindi has no '-er': the adjective stays plain and से (se) marks 'than' – सोने से सस्ती (sone se sasti) = cheaper than gold, literally 'from gold cheap'.
कहीं (kahin) normally means 'somewhere' – dropped into a comparison it means 'far': कहीं सस्ती (kahin sasti) = far cheaper.
चलता हूँ (chalta hoon = I move) is the standard 'I'm off' – present tense, no future needed. फिर मिलते हैं (phir milte hain) = 'we'll meet again' = see you.
'As sweet as that' comes out as 'sweet like that': उस जैसी मीठी नहीं (us jaisi meethi nahin) = not as sweet as that one. जैसा (jaisa) = like.
होते हैं (hote hain) signals a general truth: सेब से सस्ते होते हैं (seb se saste hote hain) = are cheaper than apples, as a rule. Plain हैं would mean these bananas, today.
मिलता है (milta hai) is literally 'is gotten': सस्ता मिलता है = you get it cheaper. Hindi frames price as availability, not as buying.
सुनाना (sunana = make hear) is सुनना (sunna = hear) with 'cause' built in: बातें सुनाते हैं (baatein sunate hain) = tells us stories, literally 'makes us hear' them.
Time and measure words stay singular after a number: हर दस साल में (har das saal mein) = every ten years, with साल (saal = year) unchanged, never सालों।
ज़्यादा (zyada = more) is optional here – कल से गर्म (kal se garam) alone already means 'hotter than yesterday'. से does the comparing by itself.
पड़ता है (padta hai) is literally 'falls' – for prices it means 'works out': टैक्सी से सस्ता पड़ता है = works out cheaper than a taxi.
बुआ (bua) is specifically your father's sister – there is no generic 'aunt'. Your mother's sister is मौसी (mausi); each side of the family gets its own word.
पैर छूता हूँ (pair chhoota hoon = I touch your feet) – bending to touch an elder's feet is the deepest respect greeting, and the phrase alone works as one, even on the phone.
गाढ़ा (gaadha) is 'thick' for liquids: दही दूध से गाढ़ा (dahi doodh se gaadha) = curd is thicker than milk. A thick book or arm is मोटा (mota) instead.
अपनी (apni = one's own) always points back to the subject: प्रिया अपनी बहन से लंबी (Priya apni behen se lambi) = taller than her OWN sister. उसकी would mean another person's.
सबसे before an adjective makes it 'most': सबसे सस्ती (sabse sasti) = cheapest; no word for 'the' is needed.
कूकर (cooker) in India means the pressure cooker – the whistling pot in every kitchen – not a stove or rice cooker.
Renting is 'taking on rent': किराए पर लेना (kiraye par lena). The thing sits 'on rent' with पर (par = on) – and renting out is किराए पर देना (dena = give).
वाला stands in for the noun: दूसरे वाले से (doosre vale se) = than the other one – no need to say होटल (hotel) twice.
Holi is played, not celebrated: होली खेलते हैं (holi khelte hain) = we play Holi. खेलना (khelna = play) is the verb for the colors and water fights.
आजकल (aajkal) means 'these days' in one word, no 'in' needed: आजकल इंटरनेट पहले से धीमा है = these days the internet is slower than before.
Elders take a plural verb out of respect: माँ stays one person but gets हैं, not है – मेरी माँ ... बनाती हैं (meri maa ... banati hain). Honorific plural marks respect, not number.
जितना (jitna = as much as) comes AFTER its noun: मिर्च जितनी तीखी नहीं (mirch jitni teekhi nahin) = not as spicy as chili – literally 'chili as-much spicy not'.
माना जाता है (mana jata hai) = 'is considered' – Hindi builds 'is done' with जाना (jana = to go): the action 'goes'. Most English 'is ...-ed' forms work this way.
Strong tea is कड़क (kadak = sharp, crisp) – कड़क चाय is the phrase at every stall. मज़बूत (mazboot = strong) is for walls and people, never for tea.
People are 'long', not tall: सबसे लंबा आदमी (sabse lamba aadmi) = the tallest man, using लंबा (lamba = long). ऊँचा (ooncha = high) is for buildings and hills.
